title: Fake Websites
about: Check a website's real name before you type anything in.

cards.prompt: This page says it's Your Bank. **Tap** each part.

parts.job: The address is what counts. Read the name just before the last .example: it's login-check, not Your Bank.
"Sign in within 10 minutes!" Pressure like this is a scam sign: it stops you checking.
It asks for your card PIN. A real bank never asks for your PIN on a web page.
A padlock only means encrypted. Scam sites get padlocks too, so it proves nothing about who owns the page.
The logo looks right, but any logo and colour can be copied in minutes. Looks prove nothing.

cards.explanation: The address, pressure, a secret, a padlock and a logo. Only the address shows who really owns the page.

cards.prompt: You type your password into this page. Who gets it?

options.text: Your Bank, because the page has its logo
options.nudge: A logo can be copied in minutes. Only the address shows who owns the page.

options.text: Nobody, because the padlock keeps it safe
options.nudge: The padlock only scrambles it on the way. It still arrives at the page's owner.

cards.explanation: The owner is the name before the last ending: `login-check`. Logos and padlocks can't change who receives what you type.
cards.hint: Which part of the page shows who really owns it?

cards.title: Read the address
cards.body:
A fake site can copy a logo, but not the real address. The **owner** is the name just before the **last ending**, like `.example`. Ignore anything after a `/`.

- `login.yourbank.example/help`: Your Bank's.
- `yourbank.example.login-check.example`: owned by **login-check**.
- `yourbank-secure.example`: a [[lookalike|lookalike-domain]].

cards.explanation: The first two end in `yourbank.example`, so they're Your Bank's. The other two are lookalikes: the name isn't exactly `yourbank`.
cards.hint: For each one, find the very last ending and read the name just before it. Is that name exactly `yourbank`?
cards.nudge: Only the name just before the very last ending counts, and it must be exactly `yourbank`.

cards.prompt: Your Bank never asks for your PIN. Tap **every** warning sign.
cards.explanation: The owner is `login-check`, the banner rushes you, and it wants your PIN. The padlock and logo prove nothing.
cards.hint: Read the address for its owner, then look for pressure and a secret.
cards.nudge: Look for the wrong owner, pressure, and a secret, one at a time.

cards.prompt: Your **password manager** only fills in on the real site.

steps.text: The page looks right, but your password manager won't fill in. Why?

choices.text: This might not be the real site
choices.consequence: Good thinking. A password manager only fills in on the real address.

choices.text: The manager is broken, so type it in
choices.consequence: It's working: it didn't know this address. Typing it in hands it over.

choices.text: Close it, then use the official app or type the address
choices.consequence: Safe. If there's really something to do, you'll see it there.

choices.text: Type it in just once, to check
choices.consequence: Once is enough for a fake site to keep your password.

cards.explanation: A quiet password manager means the address isn't the real one. Reach your account through the app, a bookmark or the typed address.
cards.hint: Where does a password manager fill in passwords? What's the safe way to reach an account?

cards.prompt: You typed your password and card number into a fake site.

steps.text: What do you do about the password?

choices.text: Wait and see if anything strange happens
choices.consequence: Waiting gives the scammer time to use it. Fast is what counts.

choices.text: Change it straight away, and tell a trusted adult
choices.consequence: Now the stolen password is useless. And it's not your fault: scams fool adults too.

steps.text: Now the card. Which number do you call?

choices.text: The help number shown on the fake page
choices.consequence: That number belongs to the scammers. Use one you found yourself.

choices.text: The number on the back of your card
choices.consequence: The bank can stop the card before anyone uses it.

cards.explanation: Change the password at once and tell a trusted adult. For the card, call the number on it, never one from the page.
cards.hint: What makes a stolen password useless? And where can you find a bank's number that a scammer didn't give you?

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- The **owner** is the name just before the very last ending.
- A **padlock** only means encrypted: scam sites get them too.
- **Try this:** bookmark the sign-in pages you use, and open them from there.

**Next:** what your apps and posts quietly reveal about you.
